newsitem.title: UK: IRA revives old fears with N.Irish police murders.
newsitem.headline: IRA revives old fears with N.Irish police murders.

text.p: A Protestant clergyman, his voice quavering and eyes filled with tears, pleaded for peace in Northern Ireland on Tuesday after trying to comfort the families of two policemen shot dead by the IRA.

"I pray God it does not go on," Presbyterian minister Malcolm Scott said, echoing fears among both Protestants and Catholics that the British province may be heading for another bout of sectarian mayhem.
The two men were shot in a side-street of the quiet rural town of Lurgan on Monday by Irish Republican Army hitmen who disappeared into a nationalist housing estate.
Politicians believe the murders were a statement of intent by the outlawed guerrillas about a peace initiative that is apparently running into the sand.
Scott spoke of the "sheer grief" of the families of policemen David Johnstone, 30, and John Graham, 34, both married with young children.

Ordinary people are praying Protestant gunmen will not slide into an old pattern, suspended during a three-year ceasefire, of shooting Irish Roman Catholic nationalists in retribution. Scott said that was the last thing his parishioner Johnstone would have wanted.
"David was somebody who had friends across the community," he told Reuters. "David's will, I would believe with all my heart, would be that the last thing anybody needs is more bereaved families."

The cold-blooded killings have shattered hopes of an early end to years of strife between republican guerrillas, who want to unite Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic, and Protestant "Loyalists" who are wedded to rule from London.
"I don't know what these people want," a middle-aged Belfast office worker said of the IRA killers. Then, with a sardonic nod, she added: "But maybe I do."

She was echoing a common view that the guerrillas' continuing use of violence defies logic at a time when its political arm, Sinn Fein, is knocking on the door of all-party peace talks. The men of violence appear to want the bloodshed to continue, come what may.

The image of the bodies, shrouded with blankets in the gentle noon sunshine, reawakened all the old fears of a society that had dared to hope politics would conquer conflict as the Irish and British governments combined to launch a search for peace.
Protestants and Catholics lived with death during long years of strife but enjoyed a rare respite during an IRA truce that lasted 17 months until February 1996.
After setting off a wave of bombs in England, the IRA opened up a second front in Northern Ireland, which for years had been its traditional theatre of operations.
It has killed two soldiers in bomb and gun attacks in the past year, but a recent six-week lull while Britain restarted arms-length contact with Sinn Fein was taken as a hopeful sign.
Those hopes crumbled in Lurgan town. On Tuesday townsfolk placed flowers outside the local police station, held a peace vigil and opened a book of condolences.
Local people are now looking down the road to the neighbouring town of Portadown, where Protestant Orangemen plan to hold a traditional march on July 6.
Many politicians fear the so-called marching season will write another dark chapter in the province, where more than 3,200 civilians, police, soldiers and guerrills have been killed since 1969.
